Thomas. One of the twelve apostles of Jesus, best known for his skepticism about the Resurrection until he encountered the risen Jesus himself. When other apostles reported seeing the risen Jesus, Thomas doubted them. He demanded physical proof, declaring he would not believe unless he saw Jesus himself and touched his wounds. A week later, he encountered the risen Jesus and immediately proclaimed absolute faith, saying "My Lord and my God!" He is often called "Doubting Thomas," though the Gospel emphasizes his transformation to complete conviction. He was also called "Didymus" in Greek, meaning "twin," suggesting he had a twin, though the twin's identity is not mentioned. When Jesus decided to raise Lazarus, Thomas proposed going to Bethany to die with Jesus, showing his courage despite his doubts. Early church tradition places him as a missionary to India or Parthia, establishing Christian communities far beyond the Mediterranean. He represents the universal human struggle with doubt and faith, making him relatable across cultures and centuries.
